fixes.explanation: Moses says Israel might say in their heart, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.” (Deuteronomy 8:17) That's the thought where you hand yourself the trophy. Right after, Moses steers them back to who really gives the power.

Forty more years of wandering isn't what Moses names in this verse. He says that if they forget the LORD and go after other gods, “…I testify against you today that you will surely perish.” (Deuteronomy 8:19) This is a heavy warning, so it's worth reading slowly.

Land loss isn't what Moses names here. He testifies about something far weightier: “…you will surely perish.” (Deuteronomy 8:19) The warning is for forgetting the LORD and going after other gods, and it deserves a slow read.

Moses says, “…just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you.” (Deuteronomy 8:5) It's a family picture. Proverbs says the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as a father disciplines the son in whom he delights. (Proverbs 3:12) Everybody understands that one.

Lakes and rain are a nice guess, but neither one shows up in this verse. Moses lists brooks and fountains and springs, flowing through the valleys and hills. I think he's picturing water on the move all over that land, which is a big change from a thirsty wilderness. (Deuteronomy 8:7, 8:15)

Nobody's haggling at a market in this verse, friend. Moses says it's “…a land where you will eat food without scarcity, where you will lack nothing…” (Deuteronomy 8:9) No deal-making is mentioned, just a land that supplies.

Moses says, “When you eat and are satisfied, you are to bless the LORD your God for the good land that He has given you.” (Deuteronomy 8:10) The moment he names is a full stomach. I'd say that's a habit that fits any kitchen, even mine after a big batch.
Moses says, “He brought you water from the rock of flint.” (Deuteronomy 8:15) A rock, friend. Most folks wouldn't walk up to a rock and ask it for a drink. That's what makes this one stand out.

The Nile is a fair guess when you're thinking of water, but this verse never names it. Moses is talking about the wilderness, and he says, “He brought you water from the rock of flint.” (Deuteronomy 8:15) Egypt's river isn't in the picture here.

Moses says the humbling and testing were “…so that in the end He might cause you to prosper.” (Deuteronomy 8:16) The hard stretch had an end in view, and that end was prospering. Forty years is a long road, so I think those two words, “in the end,” matter. (Deuteronomy 8:2)

Offerings at the tabernacle is a thoughtful guess, but this verse doesn't say it. Moses gives one reason: “…in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers even to this day.” (Deuteronomy 8:18) One reason, plainly stated, and I'll take it.
